# Question 1

The approach that I took was seeking to isolate the x term from Equation (1) to obtain $F_X^{-1}(p;\sigma,\xi, u)$, where $p=F_X(x;\sigma,\xi, u)$, namely the probability that a realisation of $X\sim GDP(\sigma,\xi, u)$ is less than or equal to x. Since $F_X$ is piecewise in the parameter $\xi$ we must perform this manipulation on the analytic forms for both the case that $\xi=0$ and $\xi\neq0$. In the case where $\xi\neq0$, we can ignore the $()_+$ function because the term in it will always be positive. This is because if $\xi>0$ the term is clearly positive and if $\xi<0$ then the term is positive for $x<x^+$, but for $\xi<0$ $x^+$ is an upper endpoint of the GPD. We will use $p\in[0,1]$ to denote the output of $F_X$.

**Case 1:** Suppose that $\xi=0$. Then we have that

\begin{align}
    F_X(x)=p=1-exp(-\frac{x-u}{\sigma}) \quad \iff  \\
    1-p=exp(-\frac{x-u}{\sigma})        \quad \iff \\
    \ln(1-p)=-(\frac{x-u}{\sigma})       \quad \iff \\
     -\sigma\ln(1-p)=x-u                  \quad \iff \\
      \ln((\frac{1}{1-p})^\sigma) + u = x.
\end{align}


**Case 2:** Suppose that $\xi\neq0$. Then we have that

\begin{align}
    F_X(x)=p=1-(1+\frac{\xi(x-u)}{\sigma})_+^{-\frac{1}{\xi}}=1-(1+\frac{\xi(x-u)}{\sigma})^{-\frac{1}{\xi}}     \quad \iff \\
    1-p=(1+\frac{\xi(x-u)}{\sigma})^{-\frac{1}{\xi}}    \quad \iff \\
    (1-p)^{-\xi}=(1+\frac{\xi(x-u)}{\sigma})            \quad \iff  \\
    (1-p)^{-\xi}-1=\frac{\xi(x-u)}{\sigma}              \quad \iff  \\
    \frac{\sigma}{\xi}[(1-p)^{-\xi}-1]=x-u              \quad \iff  \\
    \frac{\sigma}{\xi}[(1-p)^{-\xi}-1]+u=x.
\end{align}

Thus we define $$F_X^{-1}:[0,1]\to[u,x^+]$$ 
$$
p\mapsto
\begin{cases}
\ln((\frac{1}{1-p})^\sigma) + u & \textit{if} \quad \xi=0 \\
\frac{\sigma}{\xi}[(1-p)^{-\xi}-1]+u & \textit{if} \quad \xi\neq0
\end{cases}
$$

# Question 2

``` {r, echo=TRUE}
# Part (i): GPD quantile function 
qgpd <- function(p, sigma, xi, u){
stopifnot(is.numeric(p),is.numeric(sigma), is.numeric(xi), is.numeric(u), sigma>0, p>=0, p<=1) # Ensures that inputs are of appropriate form
if (xi==0) {x=log((1/(1-p))^sigma)+u} # Output if xi=0
else {x=(sigma/xi)*((1-p)^(-xi)-1)+u} # Output if xi is nonzero
return(x)
}

# Part (ii): Finding GPD quantiles for p=0.5,0.75,0.99
x_0.5 <- qgpd(p=0.5, sigma=2, xi=-0.4, u=1.5)
x_0.75 <- qgpd(p=0.75, sigma=2, xi=-0.4, u=1.5)
x_0.99 <- qgpd(p=0.99, sigma=2, xi=-0.4, u=1.5)
```
So our three quantiles are $x_{0.5}=$ `r x_0.5`,  $x_{0.75}=$ `r x_0.75`, and  $x_{0.99}=$ `r x_0.99`.

# Question 3
We generate QQ-plots comparing theoretical quantiles of a GPD for six different parameter settings, and six sets of observed samples that were purportedly generated by a GPD with such parameter settings. The broad trend indicated by the QQ plots across the 6 sets is that they tend to adhere to the GDP distribution with the parameters which they were assigned for lower quantiles, but for higher quantiles they display more divergence from their assigned distribution. Sets a, c, and f display substantial deviation from their assigned distribution of for higher quantiles, with substantially larger observed values than would be expected given their assigned GPD distribution. Since the sample size of c is very small, one cannot be highly confident that this QQ-plot indicates that the data generating process that produced set c does not follow the GPD that it was assigned, the sample size of a is also quite small and thus also would not justify high confidence, the larger sample size of f, however, justifies a greater degree of confidence that the data generating process that generated set f does not follow the GPD that it was assigned. 

The QQ-plot of set b is the one exception to the broad trend of divergence from assigned GPDs for higher quantiles; this QQ-plot indicates that the data generating process of set b is fairly well-modelled by its assigned GPD, across quantiles. Its large sample size also warrants a fairly high degree of confidence in this assertion. Lastly, the QQ-plots of sets d and e indicate that for higher quantiles, the observed values of d and e are smaller than those one would expect given their assigned GPD. Moreover, the large sample sizes of both d and e warrant a high degree of confidence in this assertion.
``` {r Question 3, echo= FALSE, fig.cap="GPD QQ-plots for the 6 sample sets"}
# Question 3


# Load data
gpd_parameters <- read.csv("gpd_parameters.csv")
gpd_samples <- read.csv("gpd_samples.csv")

# Separate the 6 sample groups into 6 data frames
separated_samples <- split(gpd_samples, gpd_samples$set_id)

# Partition (0,1) for each sample group (we exclude the endpoints because for xi>0 qgpd(1)=infty)
prob_partition <- list()
for (i in names(separated_samples)){ 
prob_partition[[i]] <- ppoints(nrow(separated_samples[[i]]))
}                                                     

# Compute theoretical quantiles for each sample group
theoretical_quantiles <- list()
for (i in names(separated_samples)) {
vpp <- as.vector(prob_partition[[i]])
# Take parameter values from sample group
sigma_i <- gpd_parameters$sigma[gpd_parameters$id==i]
u_i <- gpd_parameters$u[gpd_parameters$id==i]
xi_i  <- gpd_parameters$xi[gpd_parameters$id==i]
# Compute theoretical quantiles for sample group
theoretical_quantiles[[i]] <- qgpd(p=vpp, sigma=sigma_i, u=u_i, xi=xi_i)
}

# Create QQ plots
par(mfrow= c(2,3))
for (i in names(separated_samples)){
  qqplot(x=theoretical_quantiles[[i]], y=separated_samples[[i]]$value, xlab="Theoretical GPD Quantiles", ylab="Observed Samples", main= paste("Set",i))
  abline(a=0,b=1, col="red")
}
 

```


# Question 4
``` {r Question 4 1, echo= FALSE, fig.cap="QQ plot between all observations with flow>75 and proposed GPD model"}
# Question 4

# Extract relevant riverflow data
riverflow_data <- read.csv("riverflow_2015_2024.csv")
riverflow_75 <- riverflow_data[riverflow_data$flow>75,]


# Figure 1: QQ-plot
# Generate GPD theoretical quantiles
river_prob_partition <- ppoints(nrow(riverflow_75))
river_tqs <- qgpd(p=river_prob_partition, sigma=29.7, u=0, xi=0.62)

# Generate QQ-plot
qqplot(x=river_tqs, y=riverflow_75$flow, xlab= "Proposed GPD Model", ylab="Observed Samples with Flow>75", main= "River flow (cumecs)")
  abline(a=0,b=1, col="red") 
```
I generated a QQ-plot comparing the observed samples of river flow with flow greater than 75 cumecs, and the proposed GPD($\sigma=29.7, \xi=0.62, u=0$) model. The QQ-plot indicated that the observed samples were not well modelled by this proposed model, with observed samples larger than would be expected for the proposed model, and observed samples lower than would be expected for the highest quantiles. Outside of this small selection of high quantile values, the points on the QQ-plot are largely parallel to the y=x line, shifted in the negative direction of the x-axis. Thus, given that flow is greater than 75 for all of these observations, it seems plausible that some larger u than 0 (perhaps 75), could improve the model, although the high quantile values would still be problematic.

```{r Question 4 2, echo= FALSE, fig.cap="River flow plotted over time across observations to test independence assumption"}
# Figure 2: Plot of flow over time
plot(x=as.Date(riverflow_data$date), y=riverflow_data$flow, xlab="Date", ylab= "Flow", main= "Flow over time")

```
```{r Question 4 3, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Barchart of average flow across years to further investigate independence"}
# Figure 3: Barchart of average flow by year
year <- format(as.Date(riverflow_data$date), "%Y")
annual_flow_means <- tapply(riverflow_data$flow, year, mean)
barplot(annual_flow_means, ylim=c(0,50), xlab= "Year", ylab= "Flow", main="Average flow per year")
```
```{r Question 4 4, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Barchart of average flow by month to further investigate independence"}
# Figure 4: Barchart of average flow by month
month <- format(as.Date(riverflow_data$date), "%Y-%m")
monthly_flow_means <- tapply(riverflow_data$flow, month, mean)
barplot(monthly_flow_means, xlab= "Month", ylab= "Flow", main="Average flow per month")
```

I generated three different figures to assess the assumption that river flow is independent of time. In the first figure I plotted river flow against time, this plot is quite cluttered and noisy, and thus provided limited insight into the question of whether river flow is truly independent of time. The second figure that I generated was a barchart of average river flow across years. This barchart provided no evidence against the assumption that river flow is independent of time, as there did not seem to be substantial variation in mean river flow across years. Lastly, I generated a barchart of average river flow across months. This barchart provided reasonably strong evidence against the assumption that river flow was independent of time, with average river flow per month seeming to change in a seasonal, cyclical matter. This would violate the assumption that river flow is independent of time, while also explaining why the average across years barchart provided no evidence of this, as the same seasonal fluctuations occur each year, leading to similar averages across years.


# Question 5
I used the QQ-plot to test the fit of the model, partly because QQ-plots were fresh in my mind having just done Question 3, but also because QQ-plots provide a straightforward and intuitive way to assess the fit of observed data to a theoretical model. I found that creating the single QQ-plot for Question 4 felt very straightforward in comparison to trying to write code that could repeat for 6 QQ-plots in Question 3. I am slightly confused by the result of the QQ-plot as the vast majority of the quantiles seem to indicate that this GPD would be a good model for a larger value of u (since the points are parallel to y=x, and a larger u would simply shift the line of points down the x-axis), but then the highest quantiles seem to violate this theory, and do not seem well-modelled at all by this shifted GPD.

I produced plots 2,3 and 4 one after the other in an effort to test the assumption that river flow was constant over time. For figure 2 I naively plotted flow observations against time, which produced too noisy and cluttered a plot to provide much insight. I thus thought that grouping observation into time categories and doing a barchart of flow across these categories could be more insightful as to any dependence structure. When the third figure, a barchart with averages across years, showed no evidence of dependency, I was suspicious of this result. It seemed intuitively unlikely to me that time would have no influence upon river flow; when I thought about why this was I realised it was because I was assuming some sort of seasonal effect on river flow. Thus, I realised that year was likely the wrong category of analysis as any seasonal patterns would cancel out over the year time-scale. Thus, for my final plot I decided to generated a barchart with averages across months, in order to investivigate whether there was a seasonal effect as I hypothesized. Upon observing the barchart, it seemed to me as though I had been correct, that the means were changing in a repeating pattern across months, presumably as a result of seasonality.
